71.title: Breakfast on the beach (John 21:1–19)
71.hook: a charcoal fire, fish, and three times, do you love me
71.carry: thou knowest that I love thee
71.howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel in the Easter season and read it, with Matthew 16, as part of Peter's commission to shepherd the Church, a role they see continued in the pope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas, the doubter who said my Lord and my God. Your line was doubt can kneel too. A new week: the fire spreads. And it starts with a very small fire on a beach.

Galilee, back where it all began. Peter does what he knows. In the Douay-Rheims: "I go a fishing." Six others go with him. They fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore calls out: children, have you caught anything? No. Throw the net on the right side of the boat. They do, and the net is so full they can't haul it in. The beloved disciple looks at the shore: it is the Lord. And Peter, who can't wait for the boat, throws on his coat and jumps into the sea.
screen: `I GO A FISHING.` → `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `IT IS THE LORD.`

segments.voice: On the beach, Jesus already has a fire going, with fish on it and bread. Come and dine, he says. Here's a detail you'd miss in English. John uses the same Greek word for this charcoal fire as for the fire in the high priest's courtyard, where Peter stood warming himself and denied him three times. Same smell of smoke. After breakfast, Jesus turns to Peter. "Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these?" Peter says: "Yea, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee." Feed my lambs. He asks a second time: same answer, same charge. Then a third time, and John says Peter was grieved, because he asked him the third time. Of course he was. He'd said I don't know him three times; now he's asked do you love me three times. He answers with everything he has: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee." Jesus doesn't make him grovel. He never mentions the courtyard. Each answer comes back with a job: feed my sheep. And by the same lake where he first called Peter after another night of empty nets, two words: follow me. Catholics read this as Jesus giving Peter the care of his whole flock, part of why they see Peter, and the popes after him, as shepherd of the Church. Then they walk along the shore, Peter beside him, and the beloved disciple following behind.
screen: `A CHARCOAL FIRE, TWICE.` · `DO YOU LOVE ME? THREE TIMES.` · `EACH ANSWER GETS A JOB.` · `FOLLOW ME, AGAIN.` · then, large: `THOU KNOWEST THAT I LOVE THEE.`

segments.voice: Each of Peter's answers came back as a job: feed my sheep. Bring to mind the people who depend on you a little, at home, at work, down the street, choose one, and ask what feeding them would look like: a real meal, a message they've been waiting for, an hour of help, not a grand gesture, one plate. If you pray, you can answer the question for yourself: do you love me?
charcoal fire. The same kind that burned at Peter's denial, now cooking breakfast for him on the beach.
Your line: thou knowest that I love thee. The fire that saw the failure cooked the breakfast. See you tomorrow.

72.title: The Ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
72.hook: he goes up and two men ask why they're staring at the sky
72.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter (in many dioceses on the following Sunday), and many pray a novena, nine days of prayer, from the Ascension to Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, breakfast on the beach, and three questions by a charcoal fire. Your line was thou knowest that I love thee. Each answer came back with a job.

You've dropped someone at the airport. You've hugged, they've gone through security, and you're at the big window watching planes take off, not even sure which one is theirs. You keep looking anyway. Eventually somebody taps you on the shoulder: time to go. For forty days after Easter, Luke says, the risen Jesus kept appearing to his friends. Then, on a hill called Olivet, just outside Jerusalem, it ends. He's lifted up, a cloud takes him out of their sight, and they stand there, eleven grown men, staring at the sky.
screen: `STARING THROUGH THE AIRPORT WINDOW.` → `FORTY DAYS OF APPEARANCES.` → `A CLOUD TAKES HIM.`

segments.voice: Just before, they ask a question that shows they still don't quite get it: "Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" Is it now? He doesn't answer the when. He gives them a job: they'll receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on them, and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, and Judea, and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he goes up. While they're still looking, two men in white stand beside them and say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" He'll come back, they say, the same way you saw him go. Ascension comes from the Latin for going up, climbing. But Catholics don't hear it as Jesus leaving the building. The Church teaches that he takes our human nature, wounds and all, into the life of God, and where he's gone, Catholics hope to follow. The angels' question isn't a scolding, it's a nudge: stop staring, you've got a job. So they walk back to Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's walk, to an upstairs room, and pray together, with Mary his mother among them, for about nine days. Catholic tradition calls this wait the first novena, from the Latin novem, nine: nine days of prayer. Catholics keep the feast forty days after Easter, a Thursday, though in many places it's moved to the following Sunday.
screen: `IS IT NOW? WRONG QUESTION.` · `WITNESSES, TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `OUR NATURE TAKEN INTO GOD.` · `NINE DAYS: THE FIRST NOVENA.` · then, large: `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP TO HEAVEN?`

segments.voice: If you can, look at the sky for a moment, or picture it, and let yourself hope, or wonder, or pray, whatever is honest. Then bring your eyes back down to the room, think of one thing you've been putting off that would help someone, and picture yourself starting it. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Ascension. From the Latin for going up. Forty days after Easter, Jesus is taken up, and his friends are sent back down the hill to work. Today's word.
Your line: why stand you looking up. There's work to do down here. That's day seventy-two.

73.title: Pentecost (Acts 2:1–13)
73.hook: wind, tongues of fire, and everyone hears in their own language
73.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter; priests wear red, the Mass includes the sequence Veni Sancte Spiritus, and some Catholics pray 'Come, Holy Spirit' through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ascension, and two men in white asking why they were staring at the sky. Your line was why stand you looking up.

Jerusalem, packed for a feast. Luke says devout Jews from every nation under heaven were staying in the city. And in one upstairs room, the apostles, Mary, the women, about a hundred and twenty people in all, have been praying together for days, waiting for something they were promised and can't picture. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming." It fills the whole house. And there appear "parted tongues as it were of fire," and one rests on each of them.
screen: `A CITY FULL OF PILGRIMS.` → `A SOUND LIKE A MIGHTY WIND.` → `TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: Pentecost is Greek for fiftieth. It was already a Jewish feast, Shavuot, the feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover: a harvest festival, which Jewish tradition also links with the giving of the Law at Sinai. That's why the city was full. Now the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit, start speaking, and spill out into the street. Here's the part that's easy to miss: the miracle isn't only in the speaking. It's in the hearing. The crowd is amazed, because, as Luke says, "every man heard them speak in his own tongue." Visitors from Parthia and Media, Egypt and Rome, Crete and Arabia each hear the wonders of God in the language they grew up with. Early Christian writers noticed an echo. At the tower of Babel, in Genesis, one language broke into many and people couldn't understand each other. Here, the languages stay many, and everyone understands. Not everybody is impressed. Some laugh it off: "These men are full of new wine." It's nine in the morning. But this is the day Catholics call the birthday of the Church; the Catechism says the Church was made manifest to the world at Pentecost. The fearful group behind closed doors becomes a people sent out. On Pentecost Sunday the priest wears red, for the fire, and the Mass has an old hymn that begins, come, Holy Spirit.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `THE MIRACLE IS IN THE HEARING.` · `BABEL, UNDONE.` · `FULL OF NEW WINE?` · then, large: `EVERY MAN HEARD THEM SPEAK IN HIS OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew and Greek words for spirit can also mean breath and wind, so breathe in slowly, and out, and notice the air filling you, the way the wind filled the house. If you pray, you can say the old words the Church says today, slowly, on the breath: Come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, just keep breathing and notice what feels alive in you.
Pentecost. The fiftieth day, the Jewish feast of Weeks, when wind and fire came on the disciples and every visitor heard them in their own language. Today's word.
Your line: the birthday of the church. The languages stayed many, and everyone understood. Until tomorrow.

74.title: The first community (Acts 2:42–47)
74.hook: teaching, breaking bread, prayers, and all things in common
74.carry: they held all things in common
74.howItsDone: Catholic religious communities hold their goods in common, and parishes gather around the same four things: teaching, fellowship, the Eucharist and prayer, with collections and ministries for people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost: wind, fire, and every visitor hearing in their own language. Your line was the birthday of the church. So the Church is born. What did it actually look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

Anyone have a ladder? A cup of sugar? A ride to the airport on Thursday? The group chat for a building or a street runs on questions like that, and usually somebody answers. Now take it all the way. Luke says that after Pentecost about three thousand people were baptized in a single day. A small group from Galilee became a crowd. So what did they do next? Luke answers in one short paragraph, six verses long.
screen: `ANYONE HAVE A LADDER?` → `THREE THOUSAND IN A DAY.` → `SIX VERSES FROM LUKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of it, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." In Luke's Greek, that's four things. The apostles' teaching: they kept learning. Fellowship, the Greek word koinonia: sharing, having a part in each other. The breaking of bread: meals together, and, as Catholics read it, the Eucharist. And the prayers, including, Luke says, going up to the temple every day. They were Jews, and they kept praying where they always had. Then this: "And all they that believed, were together, and had all things common." They sold property and possessions and handed out the money to anyone in need. They ate with glad and simple hearts, Luke says, and people liked them. Now, the honest reading. This wasn't a system anyone was forced into. A few chapters later Peter tells a man that his land was his own to keep. Giving was free. Not every church since has lived exactly like this. Catholic religious life draws on it: monks and nuns vow to hold their goods in common. And the Church teaches something for everyone: the goods of the earth are meant, in the end, for all people, so what you own is also held for others. Four pillars, and one open hand.
screen: `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYERS.` · `KOINONIA: HAVING A PART IN EACH OTHER.` · `ALL THINGS COMMON, FREELY GIVEN.` · `MONKS, NUNS, AND EVERYONE ELSE.` · then, large: `AND HAD ALL THINGS COMMON.`

segments.voice: Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, and find one thing that sits unused while someone else could use it: a coat, a tool, a book, a spare hour on Saturday. Don't pick the thing that's easiest to get rid of; pick the one that would actually help someone, and hold it in your mind. If you pray, you can ask who it's meant for.
koinonia. The Greek word for fellowship, for sharing a part in each other's lives, one mark of the first believers.
Your line: they held all things in common. Glad hearts, simple hearts, open hands. Day seventy-four, done.

75.title: Stephen (Acts 6–7)
75.hook: the first to die for the faith, forgiving those who stoned him
75.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, on 26 December, and ordain deacons, tracing their ministry of service back to Stephen and the seven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first community: teaching, koinonia, bread and prayers. Your line was they held all things in common.

Acts doesn't hide the arguments. One of the early ones was about food: the Greek-speaking widows complained they were being overlooked when the daily meals were handed out. So the apostles asked the community to choose seven men to take charge of serving, and they laid hands on them. The first name on the list is Stephen. In the Douay-Rheims: "And Stephen, full of grace and fortitude, did great wonders and signs among the people." He serves tables, and he also can't stop talking about Jesus. Within a chapter, that gets him killed.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT FOOD.` → `SEVEN CHOSEN TO SERVE.` → `FULL OF GRACE AND FORTITUDE.`

segments.voice: Some men from a synagogue in Jerusalem argue with Stephen and can't win, so they bring him before the council with charges against him. Luke says everyone looking at him saw his face like the face of an angel. He gives a long speech, retelling Israel's whole story, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, and it ends hot. They're furious. Then Stephen looks up and says he sees the heavens opened and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They rush him, drag him outside the city and stone him. Luke adds a detail that will matter tomorrow: "the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man, whose name was Saul." Now listen to how Stephen dies. He prays: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then he kneels and cries out: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Those two prayers echo two things Jesus says on the cross in Luke: into thy hands, and forgive them. Stephen dies the way his teacher died. "And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord." Martyr comes from the Greek martys, a witness, the kind who testifies in court. In time, for Christians, it came to mean a witness who gives their life. Tradition calls Stephen the first. The Church keeps his feast on December twenty-sixth, the day after Christmas, and Catholics trace the order of deacons back to him and the other six.
screen: `SEVEN TO SERVE, STEPHEN FIRST.` · `A FACE LIKE AN ANGEL.` · `HE DIES THE WAY JESUS DIED.` · `MARTYS: A WITNESS IN COURT.` · then, large: `LORD, LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Let a name come to mind, someone who hurt you, not the worst, just one that still stings. You don't have to pretend it didn't happen; forgiving isn't saying it was fine, it's deciding not to keep holding the stone, so breathe out and picture setting it down. If you pray, you can use Stephen's words for that person: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge, and if today it's too much, it's enough to want to.
Martyr. From the Greek for a witness in court: someone who testifies with their life. Tradition calls Stephen the first. Today's word.
Your line: lord, lay not this sin. He forgave with the stones still coming. That's seventy-five days.

what a scholar hears: martys was a courtroom word. Stephen's name, stephanos, means crown, and his last prayers echo Jesus's in Luke 23.

76.title: The Damascus road (Acts 9:1–19)
76.hook: Saul the persecutor is knocked down, blinded, and becomes Paul
76.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on 25 January, and many use the phrase a Damascus road for any sudden turning of heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen, whom the Church calls the first martyr, praying for the people throwing the stones. Your line was lord, lay not this sin. And a young man named Saul stood holding their coats.

Saul is sure. That's the thing to understand about him. He's a devout, brilliant Pharisee, and he's certain these followers of Jesus are dangerous. After Stephen, he goes house to house in Jerusalem, dragging people off to prison. Then he asks the high priest for letters so he can do the same in Damascus, far to the north. He's on the road, nearly there, when a light from heaven flashes around him, and he falls to the ground. And a voice, in the Douay-Rheims: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?"
screen: `SAUL IS SURE.` → `LETTERS FOR DAMASCUS.` → `SAUL, SAUL, WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?`

segments.voice: Saul asks who's speaking. The answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Not my followers. Me. Catholics hear this as the heart of what the Church is, the body of Christ: hurt his people and you hurt him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and can't see a thing. His companions lead him by the hand into Damascus, where he sits three days without eating or drinking. Meanwhile, the Lord speaks to a disciple in Damascus named Ananias: go to Saul. Ananias, very reasonably, objects. This man? The one who came here to arrest us? Go, he's told; he's my chosen instrument. So Ananias goes, and his first words to the man who came to put him in chains are: "Brother Saul." He lays his hands on him, and "immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight." That's where the phrase comes from: the scales fell from my eyes. Two things the story doesn't say. There's no horse: Saul falls to the ground, but the horse comes from later paintings. And God doesn't rename him on the road. A few chapters later Acts simply says Saul was also called Paul, and from then on Luke uses Paul; some readers take them as his Jewish and Roman names. The man who came to Damascus to put people in chains spends the rest of Acts carrying the name he tried to silence. Catholics keep the feast of his conversion on January twenty-fifth.
screen: `NOT MY FOLLOWERS. ME.` · `THREE DAYS BLIND.` · `ANANIAS: BROTHER SAUL.` · `NO HORSE, NO RENAMING.` · then, large: `THERE FELL FROM HIS EYES AS IT WERE SCALES.`

segments.voice: Saul wasn't a bad man trying to do wrong; he was sure he was right. So think of something you're very sure about, especially about a person or a group, and ask gently, without forcing an answer: is there anything I'm not seeing? Then think of Ananias: is there someone you'd be afraid to call brother or sister? If you pray, you can ask to see.
Ananias. The disciple in Damascus sent to lay hands on Saul, the man he'd feared, and call him brother.
Your line: the scales fall. Ananias went anyway, and his first word was brother. Day seventy-six, in the books.

77.title: Peter and Cornelius (Acts 10)
77.hook: a vision of a sheet of animals teaches Peter that God shows no partiality
77.carry: no one is unclean to god
77.howItsDone: Catholics read the story of Peter and Cornelius in the Easter season as the opening of the Church to every nation, the root of the word catholic, universal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Damascus road: Saul knocked down, and Ananias calling him brother. Your line was the scales fall.

Two men, thirty miles apart, who would never normally share a meal. In the port city of Caesarea lives Cornelius, a Roman army officer, a centurion. He's not Jewish, but he prays to the God of Israel, gives generously to the poor, and his whole household honors God. One afternoon an angel tells him: send to the town of Joppa for a man named Peter. Around noon the next day, in Joppa, Peter goes up on a flat rooftop to pray. He's hungry; lunch is being made downstairs. And he falls into a kind of trance.
screen: `A ROMAN CENTURION WHO PRAYS.` → `SEND FOR PETER.` → `A HUNGRY MAN ON A ROOF.`

segments.voice: He sees the sky open and something like a great sheet let down by its four corners, full of every kind of animal, including ones the Law of Moses says not to eat. And a voice, in the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, Peter; kill, and eat." Peter is a faithful Jew. He refuses: he has never eaten anything unclean. The voice answers: "That which God hath cleansed, do not thou call common." This happens three times. Then the sheet is taken up, and Peter sits there puzzled. At that exact moment, Cornelius's messengers knock at the gate. Peter goes with them to Caesarea, walks into a Gentile's home, something he'd never have done before, and tells them what the vision meant. It wasn't really about food. "God hath shewed to me, to call no man common or unclean." Then: "In very deed I perceive, that God is not a respecter of persons." That old phrase translates a Greek word that literally means a face-taker, someone who judges by the face in front of them. God doesn't. While Peter is still talking, the Holy Spirit falls on Cornelius and his whole household, just as at Pentecost, and they're baptized. Catholics call this the moment the door opened to every nation, and the word catholic itself means universal. Many Jews today keep the food laws faithfully, and this story isn't a verdict on them. Its point, in Peter's own words, is people. So that was the week: the charcoal fire, the Ascension, Pentecost, koinonia, Stephen, Ananias on the Damascus road, and Peter and Cornelius, the face-taker. The fire spreads.
